panels:
The classic intelligence explosion story (Good 1965, later Bostrom and Yudkowsky) is a single software loop: an AI rewrites itself, gets smarter, rewrites itself faster. Davidson, Hadshar and MacAskill's 2025 Forethought paper keeps the core mechanism but asks which inputs to AI progress get automated, since effective compute comes from three sources: better algorithms, better chips and more chips.

The framing matters because each input has different returns, time lags and physical ceilings, and because whoever controls the automated input gains power. The paper deliberately uses 'intelligence explosion' for any period of very rapid AI progress driven by AI improving AI, not only a sudden discontinuity. A useful habit when reading forecasts: ask which loop the author has in mind and whether hardware is held fixed, because many disagreements turn out to be about that unstated assumption.

Software includes pretraining algorithms, data curation and synthetic data, post-training (RL, fine-tuning), scaffolding and inference efficiency. Its lag is short: a frontier pretraining run takes around three months, and post-training improvements can ship in weeks. Chip technology means the cognitive R&D at firms like chip designers, foundries and lithography makers: better architectures, process nodes and packaging, without building new fabs. Its lag includes design, tape-out and integrating new processes, so many months. Chip production means physically building and running more fabs, mines and power, which needs robotics and takes years per fab today.

The authors stress that lags are not fixed: once AI accelerates R&D, it can also shorten lags (faster training via efficiency gains, faster fab construction via automation). They also argue the slowest component of a loop is not necessarily the main driver of progress, so a slow fab build does not cap progress from better chip designs.

The expected order follows from how virtual each loop is. Software work happens entirely on computers, labs generate their own training data, and feedback is quick. Chip technology relies on tacit knowledge outside AI labs, diverse tasks and physical experiments. Chip production needs advanced robotics, which has advanced slowly.

Suddenness runs the other way from ceiling: a software IE could be the most abrupt because nothing physical must be built, while a full-stack IE is slower but can go much further, since it also expands the compute base. The loops stack: a software IE that fizzles can hand off to chip-technology automation, which can later hand off to industrial automation. The paper sketches three scenarios: gradual (slow full-stack IE that speeds up over time), bumpy (a fast software IE that stalls after ~3 OOMs, then slower hardware-driven growth), and rapid (6+ OOMs of software progress in months that collapses the hardware lags).

Acceleration requires that doubling a loop's input more than doubles its output after accounting for diminishing returns (the r > 1 condition). The paper's rough odds, considered loop by loop: software ~50%, chip technology ~65%, chip production ~80%. Combined, an AI-technology IE accelerates with ~75% and a full-stack IE with ~90%, but these exclude human bottlenecks such as regulation, conflict or deliberate slowdowns, so all-things-considered numbers are lower.

Ceilings, in orders of magnitude of effective compute: software ~12 (the paper also says ~13), chip technology ~6 (about 2 within the current paradigm), chip production ~5 with Earth's energy and ~9 more with all solar output. Summed: ~18+ for an AI-technology IE and ~23 (Earth) to ~32 (solar) for full stack. For speed, effective compute has grown ~10x per year; the authors call a ~100x faster pace (daily doublings) conceivable but highly uncertain.

Greenblatt's ladder (Dec 2024) defines levels by AI R&D labor acceleration: AI help equal to all staff working Y times faster, with inference spend equal to salaries and measured against Jan 2023 AI. A 3x AI resembles a knowledgeable, fast but unreliable junior engineer and gives ~1.6x overall progress; a 10x AI resembles a median frontier-lab engineer and gives ~3.2x. TEDAI dominates top experts in nearly all remote tasks, 2x faster and within 5x on cost. He later said he should have included full AI R&D automation as a level below TEDAI.

Cotra (April 2026) defines adequacy (removing humans no longer drops output to zero), parity (removing AIs hurts more than removing humans) and supremacy (removing humans increases output). She thinks AI research adequacy is very close and parity about a couple of years later. Greenblatt's 2026 medians: AI R&D parity early 2031, versus Cotra's early 2030.

The power analysis follows from who owns the bottleneck input. In a software IE, existing chips and algorithms are what matter, so power flows to whichever company or country holds the most compute and the best models when automation starts; the paper judges this most likely US-led and potentially very concentrated, even within a single company. In an AI-technology IE, the semiconductor supply chain gains indirect leverage, which brings in US allies that host critical steps such as Taiwan, South Korea, Japan and the Netherlands.

In a full-stack IE, the industrial base matters: energy, mining, construction and manufacturing capacity. The authors suggest states able to expand industry rapidly under permissive regulation could gain ground, naming China and Gulf states as likely participants. Governance implication: compute-focused policies (export controls, chip tracking) are most decisive for a software IE and less sufficient for a full-stack one, where industrial policy and energy matter too.

The authors flag several limits. The three-loop split is somewhat arbitrary; each loop could be subdivided (data generation, post-training, interconnects, packaging). Their odds and OOM estimates are explicitly very rough, and physical limits might be higher than assumed, especially for software and chip technology. Time lags can compress as AI drives innovation, so treating today's lags as fixed underestimates speed.

A strategic pitfall: much existing planning has focused on the rapid scenario. If the bumpy or gradual scenarios occur, the important decisions may fall in a slower, longer hardware phase in which industrial capacity and international politics matter more than lab-level security. Another pitfall is treating 'probability of acceleration' as 'probability of catastrophe': speed and danger are linked through how much time humans have to respond, not identical.

These prompts come from the Redwood AI futurism reading list's first week, whose key questions include what milestones to track and how timelines and takeoff modeling should shape strategy. Good answers specify an operationalization: 3x AI R&D labor acceleration is measurable through uplift studies; full automation needs a counterfactual (what if staff were removed?); expert dominance needs broad task coverage.

For the fizzle question, consider: a software IE that stops after ~3 OOMs still compresses several years of progress, may give a large lead to one actor, and shifts attention to chip and industrial loops where governments have more levers (export controls, permitting, energy). Policies tuned only to a rapid scenario, such as emergency pauses, may be mistimed in a bumpy world. A good discussion also asks which early indicators would distinguish the scenarios, for example measured software efficiency doubling times inside labs.
futurism-timelines-01.further: Read the companion Forethought papers on the software intelligence explosion and the industrial explosion, then compare with AI 2027's scenario and the AI Futures Model, which formalize the software loop. Bostrom's Superintelligence and Yudkowsky's Intelligence Explosion Microeconomics give the older single-loop framing. For governance, look at work on compute governance, export controls and AI-enabled power concentration (Forethought's coup and concentration-of-power papers). Cotra's adequacy/parity/supremacy thresholds generalize nicely to any sector and are worth applying to robotics and military domains.

panels:
Eth and Davidson (Forethought, March 2025) define a software intelligence explosion as AI becoming far more capable through software alone, with hardware held constant, in an accelerating loop. They define ASARA as AI that can substitute for any remote worker in frontier AI R&D across the full cycle: choosing questions, designing and running experiments, implementing and analyzing.

Why hold hardware fixed? It is the cleanest test of whether the software loop alone can run away, and it is conservative: in reality compute keeps growing, which raises the chance of explosion. Why it matters for governance: an SIE could deliver very capable AI before institutions adapt, and it would undermine policies that rely only on controlling chips, because capability could grow severalfold on the chips a lab already owns. The paper's scale estimate: frontier training compute could later run hundreds of thousands, then millions, of AI researcher copies in parallel.

The loop: better software makes each AI researcher smarter and cheaper to run, so the same compute supports more and better research labor, which yields faster software gains. The brake: ideas get harder to find, so each further doubling of efficiency needs more cumulative research. Economists model this with semi-endogenous growth (Jones 1995).

Two subtleties. First, parallel labor has diminishing returns: ten thousand copies working at once step on each other's toes and duplicate work. Forethought's model captures this with a parameter p (median ~0.3), so doubling parallel researchers raises research output by much less than 2x. Second, research labor quality matters as well as quantity: smarter AIs may pick better experiments (research taste), which is the main driver of fast takeoff in the AI Futures Model. Whether the loop or the brake wins is captured in r.

r is defined as the number of software-efficiency doublings per doubling of cumulative research input. In Jones-style models r = lambda / beta, where lambda is returns to adding researchers simultaneously and beta measures how quickly ideas get harder to find. If research input is itself proportional to software (because better software means more AI researchers), the dynamics depend on r: above 1 gives hyperbolic growth that diverges in finite time in the idealized model; exactly 1 gives exponential growth; below 1 gives decelerating growth.

Real systems cannot diverge: physical limits force r toward zero eventually. The practical question is whether r is above 1 at the moment of automation and how many OOMs remain before limits bite. Toy example from the paper: if doubling research input triples papers needed per doubling, r ~0.63 (fizzle); if it only raises them 1.5x, r ~1.72 (explosion).

The paper's illustration starts with a one-month software doubling after automation. With r = 0.7, each doubling takes longer: 41, 55, 74 and 100 days, still around 30x efficiency growth in the first year, far faster than today's roughly six-month doubling. With r = 3, doublings shrink: 19, 12, 7.6, 4.8 days, approaching a singularity until limits intervene.

The lesson is that the starting speed and r play different roles. The initial speedup (how much faster research goes once AIs replace humans) sets the first doubling time, while r sets whether subsequent doublings shrink or grow. Even a fizzle can be dramatic if the initial speedup is large, which is Greenblatt's point. Note also that the formula in Forethought's later model includes the parallel-labor penalty p, so the per-doubling factor is 2^(p(1/r - 1)), making the effect of r gentler than this toy illustration.

Epoch's methodology survey (Erdil, Besiroglu, Ho, 2024) is the main empirical source. Their best-quality case, Stockfish chess, uses Elo gains and testing compute on Fishtest as research input, giving r ~0.83 (standard error 0.15). Bayesian single-data-point estimates for computer vision, SAT solvers, linear programming and RL all have medians above 1 but are not statistically significant; Eth and Davidson cite image recognition ~1.4 (90% range 0.8-2.4), RL sample efficiency ~1.6, SAT ~3.5, linear programming ~1.1. The aggregate US economy is only ~0.25-0.32.

Eth and Davidson adjust upward for gains not counted in efficiency metrics (post-training, capability improvements) to get ~1-4, then down to ~0.5-2 for holding hardware fixed. Davidson and Houlden's model uses a median of 1.2 with a log-uniform range of 0.4-3.6, implying about a 60% chance progress accelerates. Epoch concludes evidence for a software singularity is not strong, largely because hardware and software progress have been entangled.

Greenblatt's May 2026 note conditions on r < 1 and still finds a large effect. First, a one-time jump: replacing human researchers with many fast AI researchers raises research input enormously. Using Forethought's model with his median parameters and r = 0.7 gives ~3.5 years of progress in the first year after full automation; measuring against AIs from ~8 months earlier (which already capture some gains) gives ~2.5 years.

Second, compute changes role. Before automation, compute buys experiments and bigger runs. After, compute also runs AI researchers and improves them, creating a subcritical feedback loop that he guesses could double to quadruple progress for a given compute growth rate (a bit more than 2x at r = 0.5). He notes a supporting AI Futures Model trajectory that narrowly misses an SIE yet moves from superhuman AI researcher to TEDAI in under a year. He adds that recent progress is mostly driven by compute (~4x/year) rather than headcount (~3x/year, worth only ~1.3x effective speed).

Compute bottleneck: much software progress may have come from experiments enabled by growing compute. Responses: efficiency gains make each experiment cheaper; small experiments predict large ones (OpenAI forecast GPT-4 properties from runs using under 1/1000th of its compute); abundant AI labor can design better experiments and catch bugs; research may shift to compute-light work like scaffolding and post-training. Counterpoint: those workarounds may themselves lower r, and returns at a fixed scale may be steeper.

Training time: a new frontier model takes months. Eth and Davidson think this delays rather than prevents an SIE, since gains can be split between shorter and bigger runs (a 30x efficiency gain as 3x shorter and 10x bigger). Davidson and Houlden's retraining variant barely changes results. Low-hanging fruit: pre-ASARA systems may already have harvested easy gains. Data quality: r estimates come from proxies such as chess and solvers, not frontier AI R&D.

Eth and Davidson's recommendations: measure software progress continuously and share it with trusted third parties as an early warning; run pre-training and pre-deployment evaluations of AI R&D automation and track real productivity; adopt threshold commitments, for example not using AI to accelerate software progress beyond ~5x the recent pace unless precautions are in place. Precautions include strong information security against state actors and model self-exfiltration, alignment and control measures (boxing, internal monitoring), and third-party oversight of high-stakes decisions.

They also argue for whistleblower protections and low-trust verification mechanisms so rivals can confirm nobody is racing ahead. Early signals of r > 1 might include internal software doubling times shrinking as AI involvement rises, uplift studies showing serial acceleration growing faster than compute, or labs reporting that AI-run research directions outperform human-set ones. The core strategic point: preparation has to precede clear signs, since by then it may be too late.
futurism-timelines-02.further: Next, read Davidson and Houlden's 'How quick and big would a software intelligence explosion be?' and try its web app, then compare with the AI Futures Model's research-taste mechanism and its b parameter. Jones (1995) and Bloom et al. (2020), 'Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?', give the economics. Erdil and Barnett's skeptical analyses and Epoch's work on algorithmic progress in language models are useful counterweights. For safety implications, connect this to AI control and to policies on internal deployment of AI R&D agents.

panels:
A takeoff model turns assumptions about inputs into a timeline. Typical inputs: growth in physical compute (investment times hardware price-performance), software efficiency growth, how AI automation speeds up R&D, and how much effective compute separates milestones. Outputs: dates for milestones and the gap between them (takeoff duration).

Effective compute is the common currency: physical FLOP times an algorithmic-efficiency multiplier, recently growing ~10x per year with roughly half from each source. Three years of progress is therefore ~1,000x effective compute, which helps translate 'years of progress' into OOMs. A key distinction in all these models is capabilities versus impact: Davidson's framework measures when AI could readily automate tasks, not when it does, and deployment lags can be long. The Redwood reading list exercises ask readers to compare models and run the web apps, precisely to expose which assumptions drive each output.

Davidson's 2023 report (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving) defines takeoff as the time from AI that could readily automate 20% of cognitive tasks (weighted by economic value) to 100%, where 'readily' means profitably within a year of engineering. Its best guess: ~10,000x (4 OOMs) more effective compute separates the two, with AGI requiring ~1e36 FLOP using 2020 algorithms at the median.

Conditional on AGI by 2100, takeoff probabilities are ~10% under 3 months (flagged as non-robust), ~25% under 1 year, ~50% under 3 years and ~80% under 10 years. Drivers: investment surges once AI is visibly valuable (~$10 trillion per year potential from 20%-AI versus ~$120 billion in AI and hardware R&D then), AI automating AI R&D before the wider economy, and spare runtime compute. With a lower 1e31 FLOP requirement, takeoff is faster (~40% under 1 year). AGI to superintelligence: best guess under a year, absent deliberate slowdown.

The AI Futures Project (Kokotajlo, Lifland, Halstead, Kastner) released the model on Dec 31, 2025, with a web app. Stage 1 extrapolates METR's coding time horizon to an Automated Coder, adjusting for slowing compute and labor growth, AI R&D automation and possible superexponential horizon growth. Stage 2 automates research taste up to a Superhuman AI Researcher. Stage 3 covers the intelligence explosion through superintelligent researchers, TED-AI and ASI.

Eli Lifland's all-things-considered AC median moved from late 2030 to mid 2032 (10th percentile ~2027.5, 90th ~2085); his chance of AC to ASI in under a year is ~30%, under three years ~60%. Daniel Kokotajlo gives about 9% to major acceleration by end of 2026. The takeoff knob b (each doubling's time relative to the previous) has median ~1.2, so the median case is not a taste-only singularity, but 38% of simulations show accelerating doublings.

Davidson and Houlden (Aug 2025) start at ASARA, defined as replacing each human researcher with 30 equally capable AIs at 30x speed, hold compute fixed, and simulate software doublings. Parameters (all sampled): initial speedup versus the 2020-2024 pace, log-uniform 2-32x, median 8x; returns r, log-uniform 0.4-3.6, median 1.2; distance to effective limits, uniform 6-16 OOMs, median ~11, derived by comparing ASARA's training compute (~1e28 FLOP) with human lifetime learning (~1e24) and adding headroom; parallel-labor penalty p, 0.15-0.6, median 0.3. Each doubling also lowers r linearly until it hits zero at the ceiling.

Results: at least 3 years of progress in a year ~60% (in 4 months ~40%); at least 10 years in a year ~20% (in 4 months ~10%). Thirty years in a year would need ~30 OOMs of headroom or a paradigm shift. They estimate ~20% chance the explosion is faster than AI 2027's median.

The rule comes straight from the model's pseudocode: the time for each software doubling equals the previous time multiplied by 2^(p(1/r - 1)). Intuition: if r > 1, each doubling of software produces more than a doubling of research labor's effectiveness, so the exponent is negative and the factor is below 1. The parallel-labor penalty p shrinks the exponent toward zero, which is why realistic values give factors close to 1.

Worked numbers: r = 1.2, p = 0.3 gives exponent 0.3 x (0.833 - 1) = -0.05, factor 2^-0.05 ~0.966, so a 30-day doubling becomes 29, then 28 days, accelerating slowly. r = 0.8 gives exponent 0.075 and factor ~1.053, slowly decelerating. Because r also decreases each doubling as limits approach, even accelerating runs eventually slow. The AI Futures Model's b is the same idea expressed directly: b < 1 means accelerating doublings.

Scope: the compute-centric framework models the whole economy and investment dynamics; the AI Futures Model focuses on AI R&D, with compute growth and explicit coding and research-taste stages; Forethought's model is software-only with compute fixed, deliberately conservative on compute but agnostic about how capability is produced.

Each handles the core crux, whether successive capability doublings get easier or harder, differently. The compute-centric model gets fast takeoff from the small 4-OOM gap plus investment surges. The AI Futures Model makes it depend on how fast research taste improves with effective compute versus how fast ideas get harder to find; the authors call the taste improvement rate the biggest driver of takeoff differences. Forethought makes it depend on r and p. The AI Futures update notes that AI 2027 implicitly had b ~0.64-0.78 (an explosion) while the new median b ~1.2 is not, which is why its takeoff slowed.

All three models stress their own limitations. Davidson and Houlden call theirs 'extremely basic', advise trusting at most one significant figure, and note that smooth-trend models underweight both tails: paradigm shifts that speed things up and stalls that stop the current paradigm. Treating capability as one scalar hides spiky profiles (strong coding, weak taste or perception), which Davidson flags may understate the difficulty gap.

The AI Futures model omits hardware R&D automation, production automation, broad economic automation and serial-speed limits; Lifland adjusts for unknown limitations and data bottlenecks toward longer timelines but faster takeoff. METR itself warns the model is very sensitive to how horizon growth is extrapolated: the doubling-difficulty parameter can move the Automated Coder date between 2028 and 2050. Parameter sampling choices matter too: Forethought samples r and p independently rather than their underlying components, a defensible but contestable choice.

These exercises come straight from the Redwood reading list: run the AI Futures Model web app and the Forethought software intelligence explosion app, share your median takeoff, and compare the models. A productive way to do it: change one parameter at a time and record the shift. In Forethought's app, r and distance to limits usually dominate; in the AI Futures app, the horizon requirement for the Automated Coder, horizon doubling time and research taste growth dominate.

Then ask what evidence would move each parameter: lab-internal software doubling times for r, uplift studies for initial speedup, scaling of research taste with compute for b, and human-brain efficiency comparisons for limits. Finally, notice correlated assumptions: short timelines often come with fast takeoff because both depend on AI R&D automation, so sampling them independently can mislead.
futurism-timelines-03.further: Read Davidson's full compute-centric report and its playground, the AI Futures Model write-up and methodology, and the AI 2027 takeoff supplement for comparison. Epoch's GATE model adds macroeconomic feedbacks; Erdil and Besiroglu's work on explosive growth is relevant. To go deeper, study semi-endogenous growth theory and the debate over research taste versus experiment compute. A good exercise is to reproduce Forethought's doubling loop in a few lines of Python and examine how sensitive results are to the ceiling parameter.

panels:
Benchmarks like MMLU, GSM8K or SWE-bench Verified typically go from low scores to saturation within one to three years, so any single one gives a short window. Forecasting needs a measure that spans many years and ideally has meaningful units, so trends can be extrapolated toward milestones such as an Automated Coder.

Two approaches dominate. Epoch's Capabilities Index statistically stitches many benchmarks into a single latent scale. METR's time horizon instead converts performance into human-time units by calibrating tasks against how long skilled professionals take. The Redwood reading list asks readers to identify their methodological differences and decide which to use for extrapolation, and whether better measures of AI R&D progress exist, such as uplift studies, lab productivity data or measured software efficiency. Daniel Kokotajlo has said he would prefer tracking coding uplift studies over METR horizons if such data existed.

ECI uses an item-response-style model: each benchmark gets a logistic curve with difficulty and slope parameters, and each model gets a latent capability, all fitted jointly from overlapping results. Models score higher when they do well on harder benchmarks. Technical details are in 'A Rosetta Stone for AI Benchmarks' (arXiv 2512.00193), funded by Google DeepMind and written with its AGI safety team, though ECI is an independent Epoch product.

The scale is anchored by fixing Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 130 and GPT-5 at 150; the anchors may be revisited and there is no maximum. Requirements: at least four benchmark results per model, scores between 0 and 1 (so Elo-style leaderboards are excluded). Domain-specific ECIs for software engineering and math exist but are scaled to the general index, so they cannot reveal different long-run trends per domain. Scores can shift slightly as new data arrive, even for unchanged models.

METR fits, for each model, a logistic curve of success probability against the log of how long each task takes skilled human baseliners, and reads off where the curve crosses 50%. The original suite had about 170 tasks across HCAST, RE-Bench and the short SWAA tasks. The headline result was a long-run doubling every ~6-7 months since 2019, with linear extrapolation reaching a one-month (167 working hours) horizon around 2030.

Recent trends are faster: the AI Futures team notes a roughly 4-month doubling time that seems to characterize the RL era. Crucially, the horizon is human-equivalent effort: an AI with a 5-hour horizon may finish such tasks in minutes. Horizons also differ by domain by orders of magnitude, and the 80% horizon comes from the same two-parameter fit, so it is not independent evidence.

Kwa's January 2026 note uses Claude Opus 4.5 as its example: a 50% horizon of about 4 hours 49 minutes with a 95% confidence interval of roughly 1 hour 49 minutes to 20 hours 25 minutes. Kwa says he could not tell whether the true value is 3.5 or 6.5 hours. Historically error bars were about 2x each way, and they widen as the suite saturates because few tasks remain above the model's level.

Relative comparisons have tighter error bars since models' performances are correlated, but differences of 10-20% are not meaningful. The robust result is the slope across many models over years. METR also notes the suite lacks enough 2+ hour tasks and planned to refresh it, add more HCAST tasks and use other methods such as randomized controlled trials. Practically: quote horizons with intervals, and compare trend lines rather than single points.

ECI strengths: broad coverage (math, coding, knowledge, reasoning), many models, independent evaluations to reduce cherry-picking, and continuity across benchmark saturation. Weaknesses: arbitrary units, no natural mapping to economic or research value, sensitivity to benchmark-specific optimization, and specialized models scoring low.

Time horizon strengths: intuitive units tied to human labor, which makes extrapolation to milestones like 'automates month-long projects' natural. Weaknesses: a narrow distribution (mostly self-contained software and research tasks), a small task count, baseline conventions, and difficulty extrapolating beyond the suite. Epoch noted at ECI's launch that +5 ECI points roughly matched one doubling of METR horizon, a useful but unstable conversion. A reasonable answer to the reading list's exercise: use horizons when you need units that map onto automation milestones, use ECI when you need breadth and robustness, and check whether both trends agree.

Greenblatt's April 2026 post argues that on large, easy-and-cheap-to-verify, low-novel-ideation software tasks (ESNI), AIs perform far beyond METR's horizon: he estimated the well-elicited 50% horizon on such tasks at one month to several years as of March 2026, roughly 20x METR's measurement and possibly over 100x. He ran autonomous projects estimated at 3-30 person-years and got what looked like 3-12 months of useful (if low-quality) work. Verifiability lets models write tests, iterate and fix errors over long periods.

He updated full AI R&D automation by end of 2028 to a bit under 30%. Conversely, METR finds visual computer-use horizons 40-100x lower than software, and a real-world coffee-making horizon of about 2 minutes. The lesson: 'the' time horizon is a property of a model and a task distribution, and research taste-heavy work may lag well behind ESNI work.

Kwa lists several misreadings. A 50% horizon of X hours does not mean tasks under X hours can be delegated; real work often needs 98%+ reliability, and 99% horizons cannot be fit without ~300 diverse tasks per time bucket and around 1% label noise. Doubling the horizon need not double automation, because failures can become more complex and costly to catch.

Tasks are low-context, well-defined and self-contained, unlike messy real projects with collaboration and existing codebases. Human baselines involve choices: excluding failed attempts, geometric versus arithmetic means (the latter would raise times ~25%), and baseliner skill, which together can shift horizons more than 1.25x. Selection bias arises because benchmark builders design tasks models nearly but cannot yet do. Finally, extrapolating to months or years is highly uncertain: whether horizons grow superexponentially is a key parameter that moves AI Futures timelines by decades.

With 2x error bars on each, intervals of roughly 2-8 hours and 2.5-10 hours overlap heavily, so a single comparison cannot establish that B is better. METR notes relative comparisons are tighter than absolute ones because the same tasks are used, but even then a ~25% gap is within the range Kwa calls not very meaningful.

Better approaches: compare a model to the trend line from many predecessors (is B above trend?), use paired task-level comparisons, or look for consistency across other measures such as ECI or domain benchmarks. The same caution applies to dramatic headlines about a single new model 'doubling' the horizon: check the interval and whether the suite is saturating. Interviewers and reviewers often probe exactly this: can you separate a robust trend from noise in one data point?
futurism-timelines-04.further: Read METR's original 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks' paper and its follow-ups on domain differences, plus Epoch's 'Rosetta Stone for AI Benchmarks'. Compare with uplift-based measures: METR's developer productivity RCT, lab system card uplift surveys and Greenblatt's notes on serial acceleration. Item response theory from psychometrics explains ECI's statistics. A natural project is to plot ECI against log time horizon for shared models and check whether the 5-points-per-doubling conversion has held.

panels:
Timeline debates are often framed as short versus long, but most serious forecasters hold wide distributions. The disagreement is about where mass sits and what drives it. Short-timeline arguments typically extrapolate capability trends (time horizons, benchmarks, compute) and assume AI R&D automation accelerates things. Long-timeline arguments emphasize that capability is not deployment, that revenue and diffusion are slower, that real-world tasks are messy, and that the last steps of automation are the hardest.

Definitions matter enormously. Erdil forecasts full automation of remote work; Cotra and Greenblatt forecast full AI R&D automation; Ord uses transformative AI, defined by civilizational impact. A forecaster could reasonably expect AI R&D automation within 5 years and full economic automation decades later. When comparing claims, first align the milestone, then compare distributions rather than single dates.

Erdil's April 2025 Epoch Gradient Updates piece (opinion, not Epoch's house view) puts the median for full remote-work automation at about 20 years, with ~30% within 10. He argues no benchmark tracks remote-work automation and 'intelligence' is too vague, so revenue is the most reliable trend, using NVIDIA data-center revenue as a proxy. Geometric extrapolation implies ~7-8 years; the linear growth seen since 2023 implies centuries; he expects something in between.

His analogy is the dot-com era, when internet revenue doubled yearly through the 1990s before slowing sharply. Assuming growth slows ~30% per doubling, timelines stretch to decades, and he says the exact slowdown figure matters less than the existence of one. He also notes AI revenue per H100-equivalent is about $10,000 per year, near world GDP per capita, and has not grown since ChatGPT. Remotable wages are roughly $20 trillion per year globally, the bar revenue would need to approach.

Moravec's paradox: tasks humans find hard (arithmetic) are easy for computers, while tasks evolution optimized (perception, motor control, agency) are hard. Erdil quantifies it as a shrinking advantage: billions of times faster at arithmetic, ~1,000x at translation, under 10x at agentic research tasks. Agentic, multimodal and long-context work makes AI slower and costlier, so he expects automating all remote work to need at least as much inference compute as the humans doing it (brains are estimated at ~1e15 FLOP/s each).

On AI R&D, he argues automating research is about as hard as automating remote work generally, and that research is bottlenecked by experiment compute and data, so scaling cognitive labor alone hits limits. Many algorithmic innovations only help at large scale. He gives only ~10% to a software-driven acceleration within a decade, though he finds a broader economic singularity after widespread automation plausible.

Narayanan and Kapoor (Knight First Amendment Institute, April 2025) describe AI as a normal technology like electricity or the internet: transformative, but on decades-long timescales shaped by institutions. They separate invention (new methods), innovation (products), adoption (individual decisions) and diffusion (society-wide change to firms, norms and laws), each with its own speed limit.

Evidence: of ~50 predictive optimization applications in high-stakes domains, most still use decades-old statistics; a widely deployed sepsis predictor missed about two-thirds of cases externally. Although 40% of US adults used generative AI by August 2024, it accounted for only 0.5-3.5% of work hours. Electrification took roughly 40 years to show in productivity statistics, because factories had to be redesigned. They argue benchmarks overstate real-world utility, describe a 'capability-reliability gap' slowing agents, and favor resilience over nonproliferation in policy. They frame this as the median outcome, not a probability claim.

In their 2025 conversation (published in Asterisk), Narayanan argues that real-world deployment limits speed: systems learn edge cases only inside real organizations doing real work, and gradual adoption provides early warning; the absence of warning would most likely signal poor measurement. Cotra worries the decisive change could happen inside AI companies over a few years, with outsiders feeling it suddenly and little time for policy.

The crux they identify is transfer: if training on games, code and simulations generalizes to open-ended tasks, the speed-limit thesis weakens. Narayanan named things that would convince him, such as a small team building a reliable but expensive shopping or wedding-planning agent, or capabilities like self-driving developed mostly in the lab. They agreed on the value of transparency about internal AI use, uplift RCTs and measuring deference to AI in roles such as procurement or team leadership.

Toby Ord's March 2026 LessWrong post argues the right response to persistent expert disagreement is a broad distribution. His transformative AI median is ~2038 with an 80% interval of 3 to 100 years, and about a 1 in 5 chance within five years. He notes Kokotajlo's own distribution (median ~2030, 80% interval 2027 to after 2050) is also broad, and that every estimate in an Epoch literature review had an 80% interval at least 50 years wide.

Implications: hedge against early arrival, but value long-payoff work such as building fields, writing books or PhDs; Ord estimates a book with a five-year horizon keeps ~80% of its expected value under his views. Greenblatt's top comment agrees on breadth but argues most people should focus on short timelines: interventions there have more leverage, the world is more similar to today, and short-timeline work transfers to long timelines better than the reverse. He put ~25% on full AI R&D automation within about 2.5 years.

Short-timeline pitfalls: reading benchmark wins as job automation, ignoring reliability and integration costs, and extrapolating fast recent trends (such as 2025 horizon doubling) without asking whether they reflect a one-off like RL scaling. Long-timeline pitfalls: assuming linear revenue growth continues, assuming diffusion must be as slow as electrification even when AI can be copied and deployed via software, and treating AI R&D automation as no easier than all remote work.

Shared pitfalls: compressing a distribution to one date (which invites dismissal when the date passes, as Ord notes), arguing past each other on different milestones, and updating too slowly or too quickly. Some 2026 evidence cuts toward faster progress, for example Greenblatt's reports of massive easy-to-verify coding tasks and his resulting shorter timelines, while diffusion into productivity statistics remains modest. Honest analysis keeps both observations in view.

Revenue per chip tests whether AI is becoming more productive per unit of compute, which Erdil sees as necessary before broad automation. Uplift studies test whether AI already accelerates the work that matters most for takeoff, AI R&D itself, which short-timeline proponents emphasize. Time horizons test raw capability growth on agentic tasks. A strong answer explains which crux each indicator addresses and what result would change your view.

Robust work across timelines might include measurement and evaluation infrastructure, AI control and monitoring methods that scale, institutional capacity in governments, information security at labs, and field-building that pays off within a few years yet compounds. The reading list's broader question is what timelines imply for strategy: short timelines favor interventions at current labs and existing governments; long timelines favor building new fields and institutions that will operate in a very different world.
futurism-timelines-05.further: Read the full 'AI as Normal Technology' essay and the authors' later responses, Erdil and Besiroglu's work on explosive growth, and the Asterisk transcript of Cotra and Narayanan. Compare with Metaculus AGI questions and the Grace et al. AI researcher surveys, whose timelines shortened markedly between rounds. For economics, look at research on general-purpose technology diffusion (electricity, computers) and the productivity J-curve. Testing your own view against forecasts from 2023-2024 that can now be scored is an instructive exercise.

panels:
Epoch's data show frontier training compute growing roughly 4x per year since around 2010, faster than Moore's law because spending grew alongside hardware efficiency. GPT-4 is estimated at ~2e25 FLOP. Hardware price-performance alone has improved roughly 1.3-1.4x per year for AI chips, so most growth comes from larger budgets, more chips and longer runs.

Two questions follow for forecasting. Supply side: can physical inputs (power, chips, data, latency) support continued 4x growth to 2030, and what would it cost? Demand side and feedback: does AI already speed up the labs building it, and by how much? The second question matters because compute growth will likely slow after 2030 as spending hits a meaningful fraction of GDP, so whether AI R&D automation arrives before that slowdown is a central crux for short versus long timelines.

Epoch's August 2024 report (Sevilla, Besiroglu, Cottier, You, Roldan, Villalobos, Erdil) examined four constraints. Power: single campuses of 1-5 GW support ~1e28-3e29 FLOP; geographically distributed training across 2-45 GW could reach ~2e28-2e30. Power is judged the most likely to bind first, given grid connection and plant construction timelines. Chips: median projection ~100M H100-equivalents for training (range 20M-400M), supporting ~9e29 FLOP; advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory are the bottlenecks.

Data: counting multimodal data but not synthetic data, 400 trillion to 20 quadrillion effective tokens, enough for ~6e28-2e32 FLOP; text alone would hit a wall in about five years at 4x scaling. Latency wall: minimum time per sequential step limits runs to ~3e30-1e32 FLOP, a later constraint. Inter-datacenter bandwidth (~4-20 Pbps by 2030) is not expected to be a major obstacle. Hardware efficiency gains, FP8 and longer runs reduce power needs.

Taking the binding constraints together, Epoch concludes runs of about 2e29 FLOP are likely feasible by 2030, a scale-up comparable to GPT-2 to GPT-4. Dividing by GPT-4's ~2e25 FLOP gives 1e4, or 10,000x. Achieving this requires hundreds of billions of dollars of infrastructure; power infrastructure alone could reach ~40% of GPU costs by 2030.

The report is careful to say feasibility is not a prediction: whether labs build these runs is an economic decision depending on returns from AI. As of 2026, announced multi-gigawatt data center projects suggest the industry is at least attempting this trajectory, but whether revenue justifies continued exponential spending is exactly the question Erdil raises. A useful habit: convert any compute claim into OOMs above GPT-4, and ask which constraint and which investment decision it depends on.

Woodruff (Redwood, March 2026) responds to the worry, voiced by Toby Ord among others, that per-task inference costs at the frontier are rising exponentially and will make automation unaffordable. He defines the cost ratio: inference cost of an average successful attempt divided by the human cost of the same task. Using METR's public data and token counts priced at OpenRouter rates, tasks near each model's 50% horizon show a median cost ratio around 3%, with no upward trend across model generations.

Among successes, cost ratios do not rise with task length. Capping budgets at 1/4 to 1/32 of human cost gives 'affordable horizon' doubling times of 3.0-3.3 months, versus ~3 months unconstrained; 80% horizons give 2.8-3.1. Caveats: selection effects (models may succeed mainly on cheap tasks), scaffold differences, and modeling assumptions to fill data gaps. He argues Ord's method overstates hourly costs 9x to 64x by dividing saturation budgets by horizons.

Greenblatt's April 2026 post separates four quantities often conflated. Serial labor acceleration: how much faster everyone would have to work, without AI, to match current output. It is the most relevant for takeoff because research is partly serial. Parallel labor acceleration: how many extra AI-free employees would match the team; much less informative, since adding people has diminishing returns. Current work acceleration: how much slower last week's work would have been without AI, which is biased by people choosing AI-suited tasks. Fraction of work done by AI, such as lines of code: hard to convert into speed.

He argues surveys should publish exact questions and time spent, target informed staff, combine qualitative evidence, and adjust for low-value tasks done only because AI makes them easy. Third-party, standardized surveys across labs would help. Narayanan and Cotra likewise agreed internal uplift RCTs and usage logs are key early warning signals.

Anthropic's Mythos Preview system card reported survey-based uplift of about 4x. Greenblatt said that, if real, it would radically shorten his timelines: median time to an Automated Coder from ~4 years to ~1.3 years, and to AI R&D parity from ~5 to ~2.5 years. But he estimated actual serial acceleration at ~1.55x (~1.75x for research engineering) and guessed informed employees would say closer to 1.5x.

His simple model: AI R&D progress scales roughly as serial labor^0.55 times compute^0.45, and about two-thirds of AI progress is algorithmic. Under it, 4x serial gives only ~1.75x overall progress, and 2x overall needs ~5x serial (the AI Futures model implies ~8x). He disputed the system card's claims that 2x progress would require an order of magnitude more uplift, and its argument that earlier models' acceleration would not reflect Mythos. Anthropic later published more detail in the Opus 4.7 system card.

Feasibility versus decision: Epoch's 2030 numbers are physical ceilings; actual scaling depends on investors seeing returns, chip supply allocations and permitting. Uplift measurement pitfalls: mixing serial and parallel measures, counting share of code, surveying people who have not thought about counterfactuals, and ignoring that AI makes some low-value tasks newly worthwhile. A 90% share of work done by AI can coexist with a 2x speedup if the remaining 10% is the bottleneck, like Amdahl's law in computing.

Cost analysis pitfalls: selection effects, in which models succeed on cheaper instances of long tasks; minimum-cost assumptions, since models optimize for success not cost; and confounds from scaffold changes. Commenters also noted benchmark overfitting could make harder tasks look cheaper. Finally, compute growth itself may slow after 2030, which matters greatly for long-run forecasts: if AI R&D automation has not arrived by then, timelines stretch.

This is Amdahl's law applied to work. If AI makes the code-writing part nearly free but writing code was only part of the job, total speedup is limited by everything else: understanding the problem, design, review, debugging AI output, waiting on experiments and coordination. If 50% of an engineer's time was code writing and AI cuts it by 80%, total time falls to 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6, a speedup of about 1.7x, even though 80% of code is AI-written.

The better question is Greenblatt's serial acceleration: how much faster would you have to work without AI to produce the same output? That captures quality, review overhead and new possibilities. METR's 2025 developer RCT, in which experienced open-source developers were measured as slower with early-2025 AI tools despite believing they were faster, is a cautionary example of why self-reports need checking.
futurism-timelines-06.further: Read the full Epoch 2030 report for its power and chip supply analysis and Epoch's later work on AI investment and data center buildouts. For uplift, see METR's developer productivity RCT, lab system cards' AI R&D sections, and Greenblatt's follow-ups on the Opus 4.7 system card. Toby Ord's essays on inference scaling costs give the opposing view to Woodruff. Amdahl's law and the economics of complementarity (O-ring models) are useful tools for reasoning about partial automation.

panels:
Davidson and Hadshar's May 2025 Forethought note defines the industrial explosion as a rapid increase in physical capabilities driven by robot factories building better robot factories, analogous to the intelligence explosion for cognition. They flag it as a rough research note and are less confident in its methods than in their other work.

The motivation is huge incentives: cheap physical labor could end hunger and disease and enable new technologies, including military ones, so states and firms will push hard. In the three-loop framework, the industrial explosion corresponds to automating chip production and the wider physical economy, enabling a full-stack intelligence explosion. Self-replication here is a property of a whole industrial system (mines, factories, power plants, robots) rather than individual robots, so the relevant growth rate is that of the entire automated physical economy.

Cognitive tasks are easier to automate first: they are less varied, have more training data and avoid real-world friction. Physical automation also improves more slowly: the authors estimate robot efficiency doubles every 1-4 years, versus AI chip price-performance roughly every two years and algorithmic efficiency roughly every year. The feedback lag is longer too: once an AI is trained, millions of copies can run almost immediately, while producing millions of robots or building a complex factory takes years.

There are offsetting factors: abundant AI cognitive labor can redesign processes and products, factories can run around the clock, and existing factories can be repurposed toward robot production early on. Historically, physical goods such as solar panels, smartphones and electric vehicles have scaled by doubling roughly every two years, showing fast physical growth is achievable when demand is strong.

Stage 1, AI-directed human labor, needs only cognitive progress: AI systems monitor and coach workers in real time, optimize processes and coordinate labor. The authors guess physical output could rise ~10x from roughly 2x more productive workers, 3x better-run organizations and 2x more people doing manual work as cognitive jobs become less valuable. Stage 2, fully autonomous robot factories, follows as human labor hits natural limits; early robots may be humanoid to fit existing workplaces, later ones more specialized.

Stage 3 is nanotechnology: because smaller machines can build copies faster (bacteria double in hours, helped by surface-area-to-volume scaling), returns favor ever-smaller actuators. The note describes these as operating at very small or atomic scales without committing to specific designs. Each stage raises both the speed and the ceiling of growth.

The note uses two approaches for the initial doubling time of an autonomous robot economy. Capital-to-output: US manufacturing produced about $2.6 trillion of value per year on about $5.4 trillion of capital in 2022 terms, implying about two years to reproduce its capital stock, which AI-driven productivity might cut by 2-4x. Humanoid payback: a robot producing ~$240k of output per year and costing ~$100k pays for itself in ~5 months; adjusting upward for the cost of building factories and the premium for building fast gives ~1-2 years.

For comparison, the world's robot stock (IFR data) most recently took about 6 years to double. The authors' real-world guess for the initial doubling is a few years, faster than today but far slower than software. These figures are rough and depend heavily on robot costs, which are uncertain.

Experience curves (Wright's law) say each doubling of cumulative production cuts unit cost by a roughly constant fraction. If cheaper robots mean more robots per dollar of reinvested output, growth accelerates: the authors estimate the number of robots doubles 1-5 times before the robot growth rate doubles, but note robot learning curve data are weak (one cited estimate comes from ARK Invest without raw data).

The long-run ceiling on speed comes from biology as proof of concept: bacteria double in hours but are too simple to bootstrap an economy; fruit flies, which have brains and complex bodies, double in days under good conditions; rats take about six weeks. The note's estimates near carrying capacity range from a few days (conservative) to a few hours (median) to under a second (aggressive, nanoscale), though the near-term path is years-long doublings shrinking toward months and weeks.

The authors expect energy, not raw materials, to be the binding constraint. Sunlight reaching Earth delivers roughly 2e17 W. Capturing 5% (1e16 W) and running robots at humanoid-like ~100 W each supports about 1e14 robots, around nine orders of magnitude above the fewer than 100,000 humanoid robots produced so far. Space-based solar collection could raise the ceiling much further, which is why Forethought's full-stack estimate goes from ~23 OOMs of effective compute with Earth-based energy to ~32 with all solar output.

Materials are abundant in comparison, since common elements dominate industrial inputs and recycling improves with automation. The practical near-term limits are different: grid connections, permitting, construction timelines and supply chains for actuators, sensors and chips. Those set the pace long before planetary energy does.

A fast industrial explosion could give a leading nation a decisive economic and military advantage, as it could out-build rivals in weapons, energy and infrastructure. This links to Forethought's power concentration concerns: a software IE concentrates power in compute owners, while an industrial explosion rewards industrial capacity and permissive regulation, which may favor different states.

For misalignment, many AI takeover routes run through control of physical infrastructure (factories, power, weapons), so a faster industrial explosion shortens the time before misaligned AI could seize physical power; Cotra similarly argues AI production supremacy would make takeover trivial if AIs wanted it. Finally, more energy, fabs and chips feed back into AI progress, closing the full-stack loop. Governance questions include monitoring robot and fab buildouts, international agreements on automated weapons production, and keeping human oversight over automated infrastructure.

Main uncertainties: robot experience curves are poorly measured; factory construction is slow and speed premiums rise sharply; other physical capital (machine tools, infrastructure) may have weaker learning curves and bottleneck growth; humans may choose not to automate fully; and regulation, labor politics and safety rules can slow deployment. The calculations involve rough scaling steps that the authors acknowledge.

For discussion, consider which features let a place build fast: existing manufacturing base, energy abundance, permitting speed, capital availability and state capacity. Three Types of Intelligence Explosion suggests states with rapid industrial expansion and permissive regulation could gain influence in a full-stack scenario. Also ask what would slow things down: chokepoints in precision components, energy grid expansion, or international agreements. Normal-technology proponents would add that diffusion into real industries historically takes decades.
futurism-timelines-07.further: Read Forethought's companion papers on the three intelligence explosions and on AI-enabled power concentration, and Cotra's milestones for AI production. For the economics, study Wright's law, capital-output ratios and endogenous growth models with automation (for example work on explosive growth by Davidson and by Erdil and Besiroglu). Robotics progress trackers, IFR robot statistics and humanoid robot cost data help calibrate. Speculative but relevant: Drexler's work on atomically precise manufacturing and analyses of self-replicating systems.
